tagline: An old pass road reshaped by California’s pumped-water reservoir
intro: East of Pacheco Pass, Route 152 descends the Diablo Range as a four-lane divided expressway beside San Luis Reservoir’s northern and eastern shores. The pass stands at 1,368 feet, linking the Santa Clara Valley with the Central Valley. Caltrans designates the stretch from the Merced–Santa Clara county line to Interstate 5 as scenic, under its program for highways through a “memorable landscape” without “visual intrusions.” The reservoir occupies the eastern slope, with the smaller O’Neill Forebay below its dam.

Andrew D. Firebaugh built a wagon road with a gentler grade across the pass in 1857. Butterfield Overland Mail coaches used the crossing from 1858 to 1861. The toll road became public after Merced and Santa Clara counties bought it in 1878 and replaced it with a new road. A later state road opened in 1923, but another realignment on the eastern slope came with San Luis Reservoir: a new four-lane expressway built in 1963–1965 bypassed the future lake basin. Part of the displaced road survives as Dinosaur Point Road.

Coming east over the pass, Dinosaur Point Road leads to Pacheco State Park south of the highway. Continue downhill beside San Luis Reservoir, then pass between San Luis Dam and O’Neill Forebay. Beyond the water, Route 152 passes the Path 15 electrical substation and reaches Interstate 5, the end of the designated scenic stretch.

moments.title: Pacheco State Park
moments.text: Pacheco State Park preserves the remaining piece of Rancho San Luis Gonzaga, a horse and cattle ranch held by the Pacheco family from 1843. Descendant Paula M. Fatjó left the land to the state, and the park was created in 1997. Its views reach the Central Valley eastward and the Santa Clara Valley westward; spring brings wildflowers. The road story is part of the park, too. A segment of Whiskey Flat Trail follows the public highway that replaced the old toll road in 1878. Cattle continue grazing park land in winter and spring, alongside its recreational use.

moments.title: San Luis Reservoir
moments.text: Most of San Luis Reservoir’s water arrives through aqueducts from other northern California rivers, even though its dam stands in the San Luis Creek valley. Water taken from the Delta reaches O’Neill Forebay below, then pumps lift it into the larger reservoir for storage. The shared state and federal facility holds water for use in the dry season. Building it changed this road as well as the valley: work to reroute Pacheco Pass Highway began in August 1962. From the Romero Overlook visitor center along Highway 152, the dam and reservoir are visible together.

moments.title: O'Neill Forebay
moments.text: O’Neill Forebay is the lower basin in a system that moves water uphill and brings it back down through turbines. Fed by the California Aqueduct and Delta–Mendota Canal, it supplies water for pumping into San Luis Reservoir. When water is released from the upper reservoir, the Gianelli plant generates electricity and the forebay receives the flow. Water can then continue downstream along the aqueduct for irrigation and other uses. The electrical system has a visible place in this waterscape: high-voltage wires cross the forebay on artificial islands, carrying power generated here and elsewhere.

practical: Pacheco State Park: Only the western 2,600 acres are open to the public; the eastern portion is closed. (checked 2026-10-11)
